tagline: An ancient land of stone and apricots
overview:
Armenia is a small, mountainous, landlocked country in the Caucasus, the rugged region between the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea where Europe and Asia meet. It borders Georgia, Azerbaijan, Iran and Türkiye. At about 29,700 km² it is roughly the size of Belgium or the US state of Maryland, and about 3 million people live there, with many more Armenians living abroad than at home.

The capital, Yerevan, is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world, founded as the fortress of Erebuni in 782 BC, decades before Rome. Its buildings are made of pink volcanic stone, and on clear days the snow-capped cone of Mount Ararat, which now lies across the border in Türkiye, fills the southern sky.

Armenia is a republic with an elected parliament and prime minister. Its people are proud of an alphabet, a church and a culture that have survived for more than 1,700 years despite conquests, exile and disaster.
landAndNature:
Almost all of Armenia sits above 1,000 meters, and its landscape is a tumble of volcanic plateaus, deep gorges and mountain ranges. Mount Aragats, an extinct volcano of about 4,090 meters, is the highest point. Lake Sevan, one of the largest high-altitude lakes in the world, covers about a twentieth of the country and is known as Armenia's "sea."

Summers are hot and dry, winters cold and snowy. Fields and orchards fill the Ararat Plain, where apricots, grapes and pomegranates ripen in the sun; the Latin name for the apricot, Prunus armeniaca, means "Armenian plum." Bezoar goats, brown bears, wolves and the rare Caucasian leopard live in the mountains, and the Armenian gull nests around Lake Sevan.
peopleAndCulture:
Armenian is a language with its own branch of the Indo-European family and its own 39-letter alphabet, created by the monk Mesrop Mashtots in the year 405. Most people belong to the Armenian Apostolic Church, and monasteries carved into cliffs, like Geghard and Tatev, are cherished places. Carved stone crosses called khachkars stand in churchyards all over the country.

Bread is central to every meal: thin lavash is baked against the walls of an underground clay oven, a tradition recognized by UNESCO. Families share dolma, grilled khorovats meat and sweet dried fruit. The duduk, a wooden flute with a haunting sound, is the national instrument. Chess is a required school subject, and Armenia has produced several world-class grandmasters.
history:
The kingdom of Urartu ruled these highlands nearly 3,000 years ago, and Armenia's own kings followed. In 301, King Tiridates III made Christianity the state religion, the first country in the world to do so. For centuries afterward, Armenia was fought over by Persians, Romans, Arabs, Mongols, Ottomans and Russians, and Armenians spread out across the Middle East and Europe.

During World War I, in 1915, the Ottoman government deported and killed more than a million Armenians, a tragedy known as the Armenian Genocide. A short-lived independent republic in 1918 was absorbed into the Soviet Union in 1920. Armenia declared independence again in 1991. Since then it has fought Azerbaijan over the region of Nagorno-Karabakh, which Azerbaijan took full control of in 2023, sending most of its Armenian population to Armenia.
funFacts: The world's oldest known leather shoe, about 5,500 years old, was found in Armenia's Areni cave, still laced up.
The same cave held the oldest known winery, where people were pressing grapes about 6,100 years ago.
Since 2011, chess has been a compulsory subject in Armenian primary schools.
The Wings of Tatev cable car, 5.7 kilometers long, set a world record for the longest nonstop reversible aerial tramway when it opened in 2010.
Yerevan is nicknamed the Pink City because its buildings are made of rose-colored volcanic tuff stone.
Roughly three times as many Armenians live outside Armenia as inside it.
